text_narrative: The new chairs are wrong and Petra sees it as soon as she sets them by the fireplace wall. They are a twelfth of full size, and everything else in the room is a sixteenth, so the seats stand as high as the mantel shelf. She puts them in the box with the lid marked for the larger house. The room keeps its own furniture, four pieces, all cut from the same rule, and the gap by the hearth stays a gap.
text_nonnarrative: Scale error in a dolls house is graded on the room, not on the piece. A chair at a twelfth among furniture at a sixteenth is a fault of the room whatever the quality of the chair. Height against a fixed feature, the mantel shelf or a door head, is the mark that counts; the rule the maker cut to is a cause, not a class. Mixed size within one house is tolerated where the rooms are separate and the seats stand apart.

text_narrative: Nobody in the workshop would buy a miniature chest from Halloran, and it was not the finish. He cut his dovetails properly, at a twelfth of the size, and they held; what he would not do was cut them at all on the drawer backs, where nothing shows. Glued butt joints, every one, and half of them split inside a winter as the wood moved. The old hands said a joint that cannot be seen is the only one worth cutting.
text_nonnarrative: A miniature chest is graded on its hidden joints and not on its face. Dovetails at the drawer front count for nothing where the backs are butted and glued: the class of the piece is fixed by the weakest joint in it. Finish bears on the cause of a split and never on the grade. Wood movement across a twelfth-scale carcase is small, so a butt joint may hold for years, which is a matter of luck and not of class.

text_narrative: A model of a three-masted barque is entered at the harbour show with the standing rigging in one gauge throughout. The shrouds and the backstays are correct at the scale, but the ratlines are the same thread, which at a hundredth reads as heavy as the shrouds themselves. The maker states the hull took nine months. The model is placed second, behind a smaller ketch whose ratlines are drawn from a single strand of the same thread.
text_nonnarrative: Rigging was graded on the ratio between gauges and not on the absolute size of the thread. Shrouds heavier than ratlines was the required relation; equal gauge throughout was a fault whatever the accuracy of the hull. Hull work bore on the cause of a low grade and never on the class of one. A single strand drawn from a larger thread counted as a gauge in its own right, so a ketch and a barque were graded alike.

text_narrative: The masts in this bottle do not fold, and Corin cannot see how they went in. No hinge at the deck, no crease in the shroud lines, no thread through the neck and no wax where a thread would have been drawn out. The bottle is whole, the neck is a finger's width, and the hull is half again as wide. Somebody built it inside, over weeks, with tools he cannot picture, or else the glass was blown around it.
text_nonnarrative: A bottled ship was classed by the means of entry and not by the finish of the hull. A hinged mast, folded flat and raised by a thread through the neck, was the standard class. Wax at the neck bore on the cause of a stiff mast and never on the class. A hull wider than the neck with no hinge at the deck fell outside the classes, and glass blown around a model counted as a bottle only by courtesy.

text_narrative: Over four club nights Beatrix brought a different wagon to the same length of track. The first ran sweetly and was found to be a sixteen-millimetre body on a thirty-two millimetre chassis, which nobody minded. The second had wheels a shade too wide in the tread and picked every check rail on the curve. The third was correct in every dimension and derailed twice, on the same joint, for reasons the club never settled. The fourth she left at home.
text_nonnarrative: Gauge compliance is graded on the track and not on the body above it. A wagon whose wheel tread is wider than the standard is out of class whatever the accuracy of its body, since the check rail sets the limit. Body scale bears on appearance and never on the class: a sixteen-millimetre superstructure over a thirty-two millimetre chassis is admissible. Derailment at a single joint is a matter of the track and not of the wagon.

text_narrative: There was a maker of miniature railways who could not get a point to throw true, and a small man came to the door about it. He asked for the loan of the workshop for a night and for nothing else, and in the morning every blade on the layout sat tight against its stock rail. He had left a thread of hair under each tie bar, and the maker never dared lift one to look.
text_nonnarrative: Four throw distances are current in miniature pointwork, of which the middle two account for nearly all commercial track. The shortest is a sixteenth of an inch at the blade tip, found on tight radius units and prone to a loose fit against the stock rail. The longest, at three sixteenths, is proper to large scale garden work, where the tie bar is a visible member. Each is supplied with a spring or a solid bar.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the club layout the scenery committee changed from dyed sawdust to nylon fibre on the whole of the west end. The fibre was applied with a charged sieve and stood upright as promised, and the west end read as meadow for the first time. By the autumn the fibre had lain down flat wherever a sleeve had brushed it. The committee recorded the change as complete and ordered sawdust for the east.
text_nonnarrative: Three grades of ground covering are held in the club store, and the coarsest is the least used. Dyed sawdust is the oldest of them: flat in section, fast to apply, and indifferent to damp. Nylon fibre is supplied in two lengths, two and four millimetres, both charged before laying and both upright unless touched. Ground foam sits between the two, sold by the litre in four colours, of which the winter mix is the palest.

text_narrative: In the first making of small things, the shaper poured all his creatures on one tree of metal and left them joined at the ankle. Each had a seam down the length of it where the two halves of the mould had met, and the seam was the mark of the maker. The second shaper filed her seams away and cut her creatures free at the joint, and none of them could be told from the other.
text_nonnarrative: Sprue gates were made in three widths, and the narrowest was reserved for figures. The wide gate stood at the thickest part of a piece, was easy to cut and left a scar requiring filler. The narrow gate lay at an edge, took a blade cleanly and left a nick rather than a scar. Mould lines were a separate matter, present on every piece from a two-part tool and absent only from the slush cast forms.

text_narrative: The figure on the desk is a soft metal casting with the flash still on it, and Dolan turns it over twice under the lamp. Flash along the back seam, heavy, and a bright cut across the base where somebody has taken a blade to the mark. The mark is what he wants and the mark is gone. He sets it down beside the other four, all of them clean, all from a mould that nobody in this town owns.
text_nonnarrative: Collectors were too hard on flash and not hard enough on softness of detail. What was called a poor casting in the price lists was usually a well-cut one carrying flash that a minute with a blade would have removed, while a figure with rounded features, past saving, went unremarked. The best of the old writing on soft metal figures was the writing that held crispness and cleanliness apart. Base marks were a collector's concern and not a founder's.

text_narrative: Anybody who paints at the long table knows which figures are Ilse's, and nobody says so to her face. She lays four thin coats where the rest of the table lays one, and then floods the whole thing with a black wash that pulls it all back to grey. The work is beautiful in the hand and vanishes at arm's length. The old painter at the end of the table keeps one of hers on the shelf and does not explain why.
text_nonnarrative: Layering is overpraised in figure painting and washing is misunderstood. What is offered as depth in the club literature is usually a loss of contrast, since every added coat narrows the range between the highest light and the deepest shadow. A wash is the opposite instrument and is treated as though it were the same one: it darkens a recess without touching a raised edge. The strongest work in the form is meant to be seen at a distance, and it is thin.

text_narrative: A club tournament in the spring was decided on a hill built in four steps of card. The defending side held the top step and claimed cover from the step below it, and the attacking side claimed the same step as open ground. Neither reading was wrong under the printed rules, which spoke of slopes and not of steps. The organisers ruled for the defenders and rebuilt the hill in plaster before the summer meeting.
text_nonnarrative: Stepped terrain is defended for the wrong reason and attacked for the wrong one too. What is praised in it is legibility, which no rule set requires; what is held against it is unrealism, which is beside the point, since a step is a notation and not a hill. The better objection is that a step invites two readings of cover at once. Sculpted slopes are no answer, being harder to read and no less arguable.

text_narrative: The tower gives sixes and Tallin has stopped pretending otherwise. Three baffles, cut and glued by hand, nothing sprung, nothing weighted, and eleven sixes in fourteen throws with three different dice. A fault in the angles, then, or in the felt, or in the room. He turns the tower to face the window instead of the wall, throws again, and gets sixes, and sits with it in his lap for a while without throwing anything.
text_nonnarrative: No count of outcomes settled whether a dice tower randomised a throw or merely concealed it. If randomising was the claim, then a tower whose baffles returned one face more often than the rest was a bad tower, and the concept held. If concealment was the claim, the same tower was a good one and bias was no objection. The two claims answered to different demands, and neither was a degree of the other.

text_narrative: Every market day for a season the turner set out four tops on the same board. The first was true to the eye and fell inside a count of ten. The second was visibly lopsided and ran the longest of the four, which he could not explain to anyone who asked. The third he weighted with a lead pin at the tip and it walked off the board every time. The fourth he kept in his coat and never spun for anybody.
text_nonnarrative: Balance in a spinning top and symmetry in one are commonly treated as a single property, and they are not. Symmetry is a fact about the body at rest; balance is a fact about the axis under rotation, and a top can want the first and have the second. If the two were one property, a lopsided top would spin badly in every case, which is not what the word means. The confusion is old and survives in the trade term itself.

text_narrative: There was a magpie who stole a boy's yo-yo and could not make it come back up the string. She took it to the mole, who said the fault was in the axle, and to the hare, who said the fault was in the wrist. Both were right, and the magpie greased the axle with beeswax and never mastered the wrist, and so had a yo-yo that slept forever and rose never. She kept it anyway, in the nest, for the shine.
text_nonnarrative: Sleep in a yo-yo and return in one stood in tension rather than in sequence, and no single axle was right for both. If sleep was the end in view, then friction at the axle was a defect and a loose fit the ideal. If return was the end, friction was the whole mechanism, and a free axle a broken one. No account of the toy that took either end as the definition of the other could hold for long.

text_narrative: In the third year of the signal service the kite works bowed the cross spar of every standard kite to one part in twelve. The order came down after a season in which the flat-sparred kites had swung badly in gusts and the message flags with them. The bowed kites flew steadier and lifted less, and the service accepted the loss. A spar broken in bowing was recorded against the bender and not against the timber.
text_nonnarrative: Lateral stability varies roughly with the square of the bow depth, measured as the sag of the spar against its chord. The constant is a property of the covering rather than of the spar, so a paper kite and a silk one of the same frame do not compare. Lift is lower in the same proportion, though only as the first power of the depth. Past a bow of one part in eight the relation is lost.

text_narrative: The first kites of the cloud lords had no tails at all, and they went up like knives and came down like them. A servant of the least of those lords tied a rag of her own skirt to the foot of one. She added a second rag, and a third, and the kite hung steady over the tower for a day and a night. The lords took the craft from her and the rags with it.
text_nonnarrative: Drag on a kite tail is proportional to its length and to the square of the airspeed, and not to the weight of the cloth. The constant of proportion is a property of the material and of the width, so a narrow tail twice as long is not the equal of a broad one. Stability is greater with drag only up to the point at which the tail trails horizontally; beyond that, added length is dead weight.

text_narrative: In the long corridor of the orbital nursery the air is still and Pell throws the same folded glider eleven times. Flat wings, and it rolls out at the third window every throw. She creases both wings up by a thumb's width and it holds the centre line the whole length of the corridor and touches the far bulkhead. A minder tells her the corridor is not for throwing and she folds the wings flatter and throws again.
text_nonnarrative: Roll stiffness in a folded glider was proportional to the dihedral angle over the small range in which paper held a crease. The constant depended on the span and on the stiffness of the sheet, not on the weight at the nose. Above about ten degrees the relation reversed, since the outer panels shed more lift than they gained, and a glider folded to twenty degrees was less steady than a flat one. Wing loading bore on neither figure.

text_narrative: Everybody who worked in the bindery knew about the third plate of the garden book, and nobody would cut it. The pivot on that spread had been set a hair off centre in the first edition, and the arch it lifted always stood crooked, leaning to the gutter. Two binders straightened it and both found it crooked again the next morning with the glue dry. After that the plate was cut as drawn and the crookedness was called part of the design.
text_nonnarrative: A single-slit pop-up consists of a base sheet, a folded riser and two pivot tabs, one glued to each leaf. The riser is attached at the gutter fold and nowhere else, so its two arms stand as a pair of levers rather than as a hinge. Tabs are absent in the simplest cut-fold forms, where the riser is cut from the leaf itself. The slit lies across the gutter at right angles, and its length fixes the height of the arch.

text_narrative: A dealer's list for the spring sale describes a printed almanac with three volvelle discs, of which the middle one is missing. The remaining discs turn freely on a knotted thread through the centre and carry a full set of month names between them. The pointer, a separate strip of card, is present and loose in the gutter. The lot is withdrawn before the sale after a second reading of the collation, which calls for four discs and not three.
text_nonnarrative: A volvelle has four parts: a fixed ground printed on the leaf, one or more rotating discs, a pin through their common centre, and a pointer. The discs are stacked in order of size, the largest lowest, and each is attached only at the centre. In the simplest forms the edge of the upper disc serves as pointer and none is fitted. Tabs at the rim are proper to the larger discs alone and stand clear of the printed scale.

text_narrative: The cut is not a cut Wren has seen before and the box has no maker's name on it. Every knob on every piece is the same knob, to the thousandth, which no steel rule die will do after the first few hundred impressions. Unless the die is not steel. She fits four pieces together and they hold without pressure, as though the board had been grown in one and parted afterwards along lines it already had.
text_nonnarrative: A cutting die for jigsaws had three members: a plywood base board, the steel rule set into it on edge, and rubber ejection strip between the rules. The rules stood proud of the base by the thickness of the puzzle board and no more. Each interlocking knob was a single bend in one rule, so the knob of one piece and the socket of its neighbour were one member. Ejection rubber was absent in the earliest dies.

text_narrative: Three sets came through the house that winter and none of them squared up. The first was cut from a board that had shrunk across the grain, so the large triangles met at the hypotenuse. The second was true but the small square was thicker than the rest and sat proud of the tray. The third was bone, cool to the hand, and made the square, the rectangle and the parallelogram without argument, and it was the one that went missing.
text_nonnarrative: The seven pieces of a tangram set were carried on a single square, and every dimension in the set was a function of that square's side. The two large triangles were each a quarter of it; the parallelogram, the small square and the medium triangle each an eighth. Thickness was independent of the plan, so a set true in outline could nonetheless be uneven in the tray. Without a tray the pieces stood in no fixed relation at all.

text_narrative: There was a joiner who built a marble run down the whole stairwell of a tall house, and it ran for as long as anyone cared to watch. He had set every chute at the same shallow fall, one in forty, and the marbles kept their speed from the top landing to the hall. The house was sold twice and the run was never taken out, and the children of the second buyers said the marbles came back up at night.
text_nonnarrative: A marble run is carried on a series of chutes, each hung at its head and resting on the next at its foot. Terminal speed on a chute is a function of the gradient and of the rolling resistance of the surface, and not of the length. At one in forty on planed wood the two are in balance and the speed is steady. Without a lip at the outer edge the chute holds the marble only below a certain speed.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the tin works the barrel of the standard motor was changed from an open form to a closed one. The open barrels had been cheap and had thrown their springs whenever a child overwound them, and the works had replaced eleven hundred in a single quarter. The closed barrels held, and the same child broke the key instead. The works recorded the change as a saving and the key as a consumable part.
text_nonnarrative: Three barrel classes are recognised in tin clockwork, and the third is a hybrid. The open barrel is distinguished by what it lacks rather than by what it holds: no cap, no arbor collar, and the spring visible along its whole length. The closed barrel is marked by the cap alone; wall thickness and spring gauge bear on neither class. The half-closed form belongs to both and to neither, since its cap is pierced and the spring shows through it.

text_narrative: In the age when the makers gave motion away, three gifts were made to the children of the plain. The first was a wheel that turned while a hand turned it, and it was honest and dull. The second was a wheel weighted at the rim that ran on after the hand was lifted, and it was the one the children kept. The third turned forever and was taken back, and the makers left no account of where it went.
text_nonnarrative: Two drive classes were held apart in tin toys, and a third stood between them. The friction drive was distinguished by the absence of any store of motion: gearing to the road wheels and nothing else. The flywheel drive was marked by mass at the rim, which was a store, and so ran on unaided. Spring drive belonged to neither, its store being in strain rather than in motion, and it was graded by winding rather than by weight.

text_narrative: The lid is shut and the catch is home and Adalin can hear the spring shift inside anyway. She holds the box on her knees in the attic light and counts to sixty, and at fifty-one the lid lifts a quarter inch and settles back. The catch has not moved. She carries the box down to the yard and leaves it on the wall, shut, and it is still shut in the morning and the spring is quiet.
text_nonnarrative: Inside the box the spring lay coiled against the floor, filling the lower two thirds of the cavity. The figure sat on top of it, head under the lid and knees to the front wall. The catch was on the right, a bent wire through the wall an inch below the rim, with its hook to the inside. The crank hole was in the left wall, low, and nothing stood between it and the spring.

text_narrative: The horse in the front room had been in the house longer than anyone in it, and it did not rock evenly. Everybody who grew up there learned to sit forward of the girth, because the bow was heavier at the tail end and would tip a rider back into the window ledge otherwise. Two generations sat forward without being told why. When it went for repair the bow came back matched and nobody liked it as much.
text_nonnarrative: On the bow the horse stands well forward of centre, the girth over the front third of the span. The two rockers lie parallel, four inches apart at the head and the same at the tail, with a stretcher under the belly. The deeper part of each curve is aft, so the low point of the arc sits behind the rider. A footboard is at the front only, and the floor under the tail end is the more worn.

text_narrative: A cottage workshop in the northern valleys was recorded in the spring as turning four thousand peg dolls in a season. Of these, the smallest were turned by the youngest hand at the lathe and were shorter by a quarter inch than the pattern. The buyer took the whole season's work at the agreed rate and sorted it afterwards by height in the warehouse. The short dolls were sold in the same boxes at the same price and no note was made of them.
text_nonnarrative: Height in turned peg dolls varied more within a single workshop than between workshops. In the sample taken across the valleys, the median was three and a quarter inches, with a spread of half an inch either way. The hand at the lathe accounted for most of that spread; the timber and the season for very little of it. Some twelve percent fell short of the trade pattern, and shortfall was commoner in the smaller shops, where one turner did all the work.

text_narrative: The arms are strung too tight and Marta knows whose work that is without looking at the mark on the neck. Elastic at that tension holds a pose for a year and then goes brittle, and the doll comes apart at the shoulder in a drawer somewhere with nobody touching it. Which is exactly what happened to the last one. She slackens the cord half a turn and hangs the doll on the rail with the others.
text_nonnarrative: Cord tension at stringing varied more between makers than between the sizes a single maker produced. Across the recorded workshops the median tension was enough to hold a raised arm for some two years, and a quarter of the sample held for less than one. Maker accounted for most of the spread; cord material for a little and doll size for almost none. Failure at the shoulder was reported four times as often as failure at the hip.

text_narrative: Over the winter in the tower the boy made four drums for the same strip of pictures. The first had slits a finger wide and the figures smeared into one another at speed. The second had slits cut with a razor and the picture was sharp and so dark that only the lamp behind it made it out. The third he cut between the two and it worked, and the fourth he never finished because the strip wore through at the join.
text_nonnarrative: A zoetrope was a slotted drum characterised by the ratio of slit width to picture width rather than by its diameter. Its resolution depended on that ratio and on nothing else in the design: a narrow slit gave a sharp image and a dim one, a wide slit the reverse. The usual proportion was a fortieth of the circumference, which was a compromise and was known to be one. Illumination was therefore external and strong, and the drum interior was pale.

text_narrative: There was a card painter who put a bird on one side of a disc and an empty cage on the other, and sold it at fairs. A woman bought it for her daughter and the child spun it and the bird was in the cage, and would not come out again however slowly the disc was turned. The painter would not take it back and painted no more cages after that season.
text_nonnarrative: A thaumatrope is a two-sided disc characterised by images that are complementary rather than sequential, which distinguishes it from every other spun toy. Its effect depends on the persistence of the eye and on the axis of spin, since the two faces must present the same way up. One image is therefore inverted in the painting, and the pair is fixed for a single direction of rotation. Threads at either edge are the usual drive.

text_narrative: In the year the guild admitted small work, the warden set the limit for a bound miniature at one inch across the board. Three of the four books entered that autumn were over it by a sixteenth and were shown outside the case. The fourth, at seven eighths, had a sewn headband no thicker than a hair and took the guild's ribbon. The limit was written into the book of the guild the following spring and never altered.
text_nonnarrative: A bound miniature is required to measure not more than one inch on the greater dimension of the board. Sewn structures are permitted at any size; adhesive spines only below three quarters of an inch. The headband, where present, is to be worked in silk and is not to stand above the head of the board. Boards are to be of paper or of thin wood, and leather over board is required in the closed class.

text_narrative: When the first station was hung above the world, its builders made a window that looked on a garden. The garden was three feet deep and read as a mile, because the trees at the back were a fortieth of the trees at the front and the path narrowed all the way to a painted hill. Every child born there believed in the hill, and none of them could say afterwards when they had stopped.
text_nonnarrative: Depth in a forced diorama was required to be graded in not fewer than four planes. A scale ratio of more than one to three between adjacent planes was not permitted, since the step read as a step. The rear plane was to be painted and was not to carry a modelled figure of any size. Viewing was permitted from one aperture only, and the aperture was to be fixed in height and not adjustable.

text_narrative: At the kitchen table Rosalind twists sixty strands of florist wire into a trunk and splits them off in threes. The lower branches come out fine and the crown runs out of wire, so the top of the tree is four bare stems where there should be forty. She adds a second bundle at the fork and binds the join with thread. The tree stands in the vice overnight with the join at eye level, plain as a splice on a rope.
text_nonnarrative: Wire armatures were the wrong method for model trees and the only practical one. The objection to them was structural: the number of strands had to be settled before the first twist, and no number settled that early could match the branching of a crown. Against this it was often said that a modeller could add a second bundle of wire at any fork. So a modeller could, and the join showed at every attempt, and the objection stood unanswered.

text_narrative: The duck on wheels that went round the estate for thirty years was never quiet and never the same twice. Whoever had it would swear the clack changed with the weather, faster in the dry, slower and heavier when the rain came, and nobody ever oiled it. It went through nine families and came back to the first one with the cam worn to a smooth oval that should not have clacked at all. It clacked.
text_nonnarrative: The clacking pull-along is dismissed as a noise toy, and the dismissal misses the mechanism. Noise is the effect but not the function: the cam under the axle converts steady rolling into an irregular beat, and the irregularity holds attention where a bell would not. It may be objected that the beat is regular after all, being fixed by the cam. Fixed it is, and irregular against the walking of the child, which is the frame that matters.

text_narrative: A parlour skittles set entered for the county fair was measured on the morning of the second day. Eight of the nine pins stood to the pattern; the ninth was heavier at the base by two ounces of sand under a plugged foot. The owner said the pin had been rebuilt after a split and the sand was there for weight and not for advantage. The set was shown as a working set and not as a matched set.
text_nonnarrative: Ballast: any weight added inside the foot of a pin after turning, whether of sand, shot or plaster. Plug: the disc closing the cavity, flush with the foot and of the same timber as the pin. Matched set: nine pins of which no two differed in weight by more than half an ounce. Working set: any set outside that tolerance but sound in foot and head. Dead pin: one whose ballast had shifted and lay loose in the cavity.

text_narrative: Three rods for two arms, and Enid has counted them twice against the screen. The elbow rod is the one that should not be there, because this figure was cut with the elbow fixed and she cut it herself in the spring. Somebody has pierced the joint and set a rod in it, and the pierce is clean and old. She works the new rod once and the shadow arm bends the wrong way at the elbow, backwards, like nothing that walks.
text_nonnarrative: Control rod: the fixed stave at the trunk, carrying the whole weight of a figure. Action rod: any rod at a limb, jointed to it at one end and free at the other. Live joint: a pierced joint with an action rod fitted, the limb turning about the pierce. Dead joint: the same pierce with no rod, or a joint cut solid in the hide. Reverse: any live joint whose travel lay outside the range of the joint it stood for.

text_narrative: Across three exhibitions Nell shows the same window at a twentieth scale and is asked the same question at each. At the first the panel is leaded in drawn wire and the steward enters it under glass. At the second the wire is flat-rolled and the steward enters it under metalwork. At the third the panel is unchanged and the steward asks her which she would prefer, and she says glass, and it goes under glass and takes nothing.
text_nonnarrative: A leaded miniature means, in this schedule, a glazed panel under nine inches in either dimension in which the calmes are of lead or of lead alloy. Drawn wire of round section does not fall within the definition, and a panel so made is entered as metalwork. Where a panel carries both round wire and flat calme, the greater length by measure governs. Nothing in this schedule affects the classification of painted glass carrying no calmes at all.

text_narrative: There was a saddler's widow who stuffed hobby horse heads with horsehair and would use nothing else. A fox came to the door in a coat and offered her a sack of wool at half the price, and she took it, and the heads went soft inside a month and hung on their sticks like sacks. She bought no more wool, and the fox was seen at the next village with a sack of horsehair.
text_nonnarrative: A stuffed head means a hobby horse head filled with a resilient material, resilience being recovery after compression and not density. Horsehair, tow and curled paper are within the definition; wool and rag are not, being non-resilient however tightly packed. Where a head is filled with two materials, the material at the muzzle governs. Nothing in this part applies to a head of carved wood, which is not a filled head at all.

text_narrative: In the third year of the camp the model club fixed the rib spacing for hull work at four matchsticks to the inch. Two entries that season were built at three and were shown but not entered, and one at six collapsed under its own deck before the show. The four-stick rule held for the rest of the war and was written on the workshop wall in pencil. Nobody recorded who set it.
text_nonnarrative: A hull was admissible only where the rib spacing lay between three and five sticks to the inch. A hull outside that band stood outside the class and could not be answered by a hull inside it. Spacing was counted at the widest frame and nowhere else, so a tapered hull was legal on one count and not on another. Collapse under deck weight was a defect of the joint and bore on no rule.

text_narrative: In the time before hair was given to the made people, their heads were painted and their makers were content. One maker, the least of them, knotted a single strand through a pierced scalp and drew it tight, and then another, and did not stop for nine days. The made thing she finished was the first to be wept over, and the others were put away unfinished. After that no head was painted again.
text_nonnarrative: A knot counted as set only where it lay flat against the scalp and held against a pull of one ounce. Two strands through a single pierce were not two knots and could not be counted as such. A scalp in which the pierces stood closer than a sixteenth of an inch was void, whatever the number of knots in it. Painted hair was not hair and was answerable to no rule of knotting at all.
